title: Comma Cottage
intro: The comma rules that quietly wreck a good sentence.

options: I bought apples, bananas and milk.
I bought apples bananas and milk.
I bought, apples, bananas, and, milk.
Come here, John.
Come here John.
Come, here John.
No, I don't want any.
No I don't want any.
No, I don't, want any.

A2.q: Joining two short ideas with ‘but’ — which is correct?
options: I was tired, but I kept working.
I was tired but, I kept working.
I was tired, but I kept, working.
Well, that's interesting.
Well that's interesting.
Well, that's, interesting.
Also, I forgot my keys.
Also I forgot my keys.
Also, I, forgot my keys.

A2.q: Thanking someone by name — which is correct?
options: Thank you, Maria.
Thank you Maria.
Thank, you Maria.
Firstly, let's discuss the budget.
Firstly let's discuss the budget.
Firstly, let's, discuss the budget.

A2.q: A list of three adjectives — which is correct?
options: She is kind, honest and generous.
She is kind honest and generous.
She is kind, honest, and, generous.

B1.q: Long introductory clause — which is correct?
options: After finishing his homework, he went outside to play.
After finishing his homework he went outside to play.
After finishing, his homework he went outside to play.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I was tired, I went to bed early.
I was tired I went to bed, early.

B1.q: Joining two full sentences — which is correct?
options: She studied hard, and she passed the exam.
She studied hard she passed the exam.
She studied hard, she passed the exam.

B1.q: Non-essential extra information — which is correct?
options: My brother, who lives in London, is visiting next week.
My brother who lives in London is visiting next week.
My brother, who lives in London is visiting next week.
It was raining, but we still went for a walk.
It was raining, we still went for a walk.
It was raining we still went, for a walk.
In spite of the rain, the match continued.
In spite of the rain the match continued.
In spite, of the rain, the match continued.

B1.q: Two independent clauses, no conjunction — which is correct?
options: The shop was closed; we went home.
The shop was closed, we went home.
The shop was closed we went, home.
First, we checked in. Then, we found our seats.
First we checked in. Then we found our seats.
First, we, checked in. Then, we, found our seats.

B1.q: Introducing a direct quotation — which is correct?
options: She said, "I'll be there at six."
She said "I'll be there at six."
She said, "I'll, be there at six."

B2.q: A necessary Oxford comma — which avoids confusion about who the parents are?
options: I'd like to thank my parents, Sara, and Hugo.
I'd like to thank my parents, Sara and Hugo.
I'd like to thank my parents Sara and Hugo.

B2.q: Non-defining relative clause — which is correct?
options: Valencia, which is on the Mediterranean coast, is famous for paella.
Valencia which is on the Mediterranean coast is famous for paella.
Valencia, which is on the Mediterranean coast is famous for paella.
The results, to be honest, were disappointing.
The results to be honest were disappointing.
The results, to be honest were disappointing.

B2.q: Comma before a contrasting phrase — which is correct?
options: The plan was ambitious, though ultimately unsuccessful.
The plan was ambitious though ultimately unsuccessful.
The plan was ambitious, though, ultimately unsuccessful.
Her work finished, she left the office early.
Her work finished she left the office early.
Her work, finished, she left the office early.

B2.q: Comma with a coordinating conjunction — which is correct?
options: He wanted to travel, yet he never had the money.
He wanted to travel yet he never had the money.
He wanted to travel, yet, he never had the money.

B2.q: Direct address mid-sentence — which is correct?
options: I think, Maria, that you're right.
I think Maria that you're right.
I think, Maria that you're right.

B2.q: Comma splice with a long clause — which is correct?
options: The negotiations continued for hours; neither side would compromise.
The negotiations continued for hours, neither side would compromise.
The negotiations continued for hours neither side, would compromise.

B2.q: Comma after a conditional clause — which is correct?
options: If the weather improves, we'll go to the beach.
If the weather improves we'll go to the beach.
If the weather, improves, we'll go to the beach.

C1.q: Identifying one specific report — which is correct?
options: The report that was published last week caused controversy.
The report, that was published last week, caused controversy.
The report which was published last week, caused controversy.
The results, however, tell a different story.
The results however tell a different story.
The results, however tell a different story.

C1.q: A comma before ‘because’ is usually wrong — which is correct?
options: She left early because she felt unwell.
She left early, because she felt unwell.
She left, early because she felt unwell.

C1.q: Comma with an appositive — which is correct?
options: Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote, was born in Alcalá de Henares.
Cervantes the author of Don Quixote was born in Alcalá de Henares.
Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote was born in Alcalá de Henares.

C1.q: A series of independent clauses — which is correct?
options: The board reviewed the proposal, debated its merits, and rejected it.
The board reviewed the proposal, debated its merits and, rejected it.
The board reviewed the proposal debated its merits and rejected it.

C1.q: ‘Not only… but also’ — which is correct?
options: The policy was not only unpopular, but also unworkable.
The policy was not only unpopular but, also unworkable.
The policy was, not only unpopular but also unworkable.

C1.q: Dashes instead of commas — which is correct?
options: The proposal — controversial from the start — was eventually withdrawn.
The proposal, controversial from the start — was eventually withdrawn.
The proposal — controversial from the start, was eventually withdrawn.

C1.q: Comma splice in formal writing — which is correct?
options: The data was inconclusive; further research is required.
The data was inconclusive, further research is required.
The data was inconclusive further, research is required.

C1.q: Comma after a long subordinate clause — which is correct?
options: Although the committee had reservations about the budget, they approved the project.
Although the committee had reservations about the budget they approved the project.
Although the committee had reservations, about the budget, they approved the project.
